Affiliation:: Advanced Radar Research Center (ARRC); School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The University of Oklahoma (OU); Norman, OK, USA; also affiliated with OU Meteorology
Research Domains: Large-scale antenna array design and calibration
Mutual coupling-based calibration and in-field calibration methods
High-throughput data handling and real-time signal processing for radar
Radar system validation with field experiments and comparison against legacy systems
Interdisciplinary applications bridging radar science with ML/security research
Techniques Used: Fully digital, element-level beamforming with FPGA-based processing
Polarimetric radar calibration methods including mutual coupling, boresight corrections, and cross-polar cancellation
Near-field and UAS-based far-field calibration techniques
S-band Horus PAR architecture with 1600 radiating elements organized into 25 panels (8×8 elements per panel)
MVDR beamforming and Space-Time Adaptive Processing (STAP) concepts for interference suppression
Progressive pulse compression for improved range resolution
High-throughput data handling with RapidIO interconnect and PCIe data ingestion
Software-defined radar architecture enabling multi-mission reconfigurability
Phase-only and phase-plus-amplitude beamforming with optimization methods such as Bézier-surface parameterization (as demonstrated in Horus MSB work)
Data & Platforms: Horus fully digital polarimetric PAR experiments at OU ARRC; collaboration with NOAA/NSSL
Hardware: 1600 dual-polarization elements, 8×8 panel tiles, AD9371 transceivers, Arria 10 FPGAs, Cyclone V SoC, DDR4 memory, RapidIO interconnect
Measurement and validation tools: near-field Velmex scanner, UAS-based far-field calibration (RF-Sonde), anechoic chamber measurements
Software and analysis: MATLAB (GA-based pattern synthesis in Horus studies), HFSS panel simulations (element/panel validation)
Data characteristics: high data rates (theoretical up to 1.5 Gbps), large-scale datasets (multi-terabyte scale in field campaigns)
Application Areas: Next-generation weather observation and hydrometeor classification
High-temporal-resolution polarimetric weather sensing for QPE
Airborne and ground-based remote sensing with software-defined radar
DARPA BLiP program context for Beyond Linear Processing and non-linear signal processing readiness
Interdisciplinary collaborations spanning radar engineering, meteorology, and ML-based security/robustness research
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Systems-level integration: co-design of hardware architecture, software, calibration, and data management for scalable radar arrays
Field-driven validation: combining near-field, far-field, and in-field meteorological data to verify calibration and performance
Scalability and reproducibility: modular panel-based architecture enabling large-element-count deployments and repeatable experiments
Cross-disciplinary exploration: bridging radar technology with machine learning and security-oriented research to broaden impact
Optimization-driven design: leveraging optimization (GA, Bézier parameterization) to explore trade-offs between beam quality, agility, and data handling
Summary Description: Dr. Mark Yeary leads pivotal work at OU’s Advanced Radar Research Center on next-generation, fully digital polarimetric weather radars (notably Horus). His contributions span the design and evaluation of large-scale PAR architectures, distributed and software-defined beamforming, real-time data handling, and robust calibration via mutual coupling and UAS-based calibration techniques. This work enables high-fidelity, high-temporal-resolution polarimetric weather observations and scalable deployment strategies. In addition to radar-focused efforts, his collaboration on interdisciplinary topics—such as ML-enabled security research—highlights a breadth of methodological expertise and a commitment to advancing sensing technologies through robust, field-tested, and scalable solutions.
